questions.question: For an eigenvalue λ of A, what condition allows v to be called a generalized eigenvector?
options: There is a positive integer k such that $(A-λI)^k v=0$.
The vector v is perpendicular to every ordinary eigenvector.
$(A-λI)v=v$ for every vector v.
There is a positive integer k such that $A^k v=λv$.
questions.explanation: $v$ is a generalized eigenvector for $\lambda$ if $(A-\lambda I)^k v=0$ for some positive integer $k$.
questions.source_support: Definition: a generalized eigenvector satisfies $(A-λI)^k v=0$ for some positive integer k.
questions.skill_detail: Recognise the defining condition for a generalized eigenvector.
option_explanations: It need not be perpendicular to ordinary eigenvectors.
$(A-\lambda I)v=v$ is not the condition.
$A^k v=\lambda v$ is not the defining condition.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is every ordinary eigenvector also a generalized eigenvector?
options: It is automatically an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.
It already satisfies $(A-λI)v=0$, so k=1 works.
It satisfies $(A-λI)v=v$, so k=0 works.
It has to be linearly independent from all other eigenvectors.
questions.explanation: An ordinary eigenvector satisfies $(A-\lambda I)v=0$, which is the generalized condition with $k=1$.
questions.source_support: Relevant result: every ordinary eigenvector is a generalized eigenvector with k=1.

option_explanations: It is not an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.

Linear independence is not the reason.

It is any vector outside the domain of $A$.

questions.question: Why must the integer k in $(A-λI)^k v=0$ be positive?
options: The condition is about applying $A-λI$ at least once.
The condition is about choosing k equal to the matrix size only.
The condition is about making λ positive.
The condition is about taking a negative power of $A-λI$.
questions.explanation: $k$ must be positive because the condition $(A-\lambda I)^k v=0$ requires applying $A-\lambda I$ at least once ($k\ge 1$); $k=0$ would give $Iv=v\ne 0$.
questions.source_support: Definition: k is a positive integer.
questions.skill_detail: Recall the role of k in the definition.
option_explanations: $k$ need not equal the matrix size; $k$ can be any positive integer for which $(A-\lambda I)^k v=0$, often smaller than $n$.
It does not make $\lambda$ positive; $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue (any scalar), and $k$ is the exponent in $(A-\lambda I)^k$, with no connection to the sign of $\lambda$.
It does not take a negative power of $A-\lambda I$; $k\ge 1$ is a positive power, and negative powers would require invertibility.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
